paras: The killing of William Jones was the fatal shooting of a Black man by James Ross, a white man, at Ross's house in Nashville, Tennessee, on Sunday, August 7, 1881. By the account sent over the wires, Jones had gone to ask Ross why he had hit a Black boy with a stone, and Ross answered by fetching a pistol and shooting him dead. The story ran as a short item in crime roundups across the country, while a Memphis paper printed a version in which Jones struck Ross first.

According to the Nashville dispatch, Ross had earlier that day hit a "colored boy" in the back with a stone. The Morristown Gazette, a Tennessee weekly, added that he did so "for impudent language." The Memphis Daily Appeal described the cause differently, saying Ross had been "chastising some colored children for committing nuisances" near a spring on his premises.

Jones afterward went to Ross's house and asked why he had treated the boy that way. In the wire version, Ross asked him what he had to do with it, ran into the house, got a pistol and shot Jones dead. The St. Paul Daily Globe's text said Ross "drew a revolver," and the Morristown Gazette said he got his pistol "immediately." No report gives the time of day or mentions onlookers.
No report of Ross's arrest, an inquest, an indictment or a trial was found in the coverage, the last of which ran in mid-August.

The killing reached readers chiefly through a Nashville dispatch dated August 7, printed the next day in Washington, Wheeling, St. Paul and Sacramento papers. Headline writers labeled it "A COLORED MAN SHOT DEAD.", "COLORED SHOOTING.", "A Nashville Tragedy" and "Homicide at Nashville," and the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer set it in a roundup under the line that "the Epidemic of Murder Shows no Abatement." Every version named Ross as white and Jones as "colored," without comment on the shooting itself.

As the item was cut down for weekly columns, Jones's part shifted. The Canton Advocate said Ross killed "a negro named William Jones for interfering in a quarrel," and the Dallas Daily Herald said Jones, "a colored citizen," was shot "for interfering with the punishment of a lad." The Stark County Democrat called the killing "the result of a quarrel," and the "Tragical Tales" column reprinted in Wisconsin and Minnesota weeklies gave only names, races, place and date. No Nashville paper's account appears in the coverage.

Accounts differ on who used violence first at Ross's house. The wire dispatch, followed by the Morristown Gazette, mentions no violence by Jones before Ross fetched his pistol. The Memphis Daily Appeal said Jones, after "a war of words," assaulted Ross with a stone, with Ross "getting the drop" on him with his pistol; the paper did not name its source.

reader.title: Killing of William Jones (Nashville, 1881)
bases: Every report describes one white man, James Ross, shooting one Black man, William Jones, in a personal dispute at Ross's house; no mob, band or officers appear (A1, A10, A14).

The Nashville wire dispatch (A1, A4, A7) and a separately worded Memphis Daily Appeal account (A10) agree that Ross shot and killed Jones at Nashville on Sunday, August 7, though they differ on how the quarrel began and who struck first.

accounts.gist: Ross hit a colored boy in the back with a stone; Jones later went to Ross's house and asked why; Ross asked what he had to do with it, ran into the house, got a pistol and shot Jones dead.

accounts.label: Morristown Gazette (Tennessee) version
accounts.gist: Follows the wire but adds that Ross stoned the boy 'for impudent language' and that Ross 'immediately' got his pistol.

accounts.label: Memphis Daily Appeal version
accounts.gist: Ross had been chastising colored children for committing nuisances near a spring on his premises; Jones took the children's part, went to Ross's house and after a 'war of words' assaulted Ross with a stone, and Ross 'got the drop' on him with a pistol.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Nashville dispatch verbatim or cut to one line, under headings such as 'A COLORED MAN SHOT DEAD.', 'COLORED SHOOTING.' and 'Homicide at Nashville', identifying Ross as white and Jones as colored without comment.

Condensed versions reframed Jones's role as 'interfering in a quarrel' or 'interfering with the punishment of a lad', and the Memphis Daily Appeal printed a version in which Jones attacked Ross first.
